## QUESTION 1

__Write an SQL query that pulls in the the salaries table and the collegeplaying table (and any other tables you might need) and store them in polars dataframes. In Python Polars, combine the dataframes to create a list of baseball players who attended BYU-Idaho. The new table should contain five columns: playerID, schoolID, salary, yearID and teamID associated with each salary.__

The table below shows all salary records for players who attended BYU-Idaho (`idbyuid`). Each row includes the player, their school, and the salary they earned in a specific year and team. Since some players appear multiple times in the `collegeplaying` table, I first reduced the data to unique `playerID` and `schoolID` pairs so that the same salary would not be counted more than once. One thing I noticed is that only a few players in the database attended BYU-Idaho, but those who did were able to play in Major League Baseball and earn salaries over several seasons.


```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
pl.read_database("SELECT schoolID, name_full FROM schools WHERE name_full LIKE '%Idaho%'", con)
salaries = pl.read_database("SELECT playerID, yearID, teamID, salary FROM salaries", con)
college  = pl.read_database("SELECT playerID, schoolID FROM collegeplaying", con)
byui = (college
    .filter(pl.col("schoolID") == "idbyuid")
    .select(["playerID", "schoolID"])
    .unique())
byui_salaries = (salaries
    .join(byui, on="playerID", how="inner")
    .select(["playerID", "schoolID", "salary", "yearID", "teamID"])
    .sort(["playerID", "yearID"]))

byui_salaries
```


## QUESTION 2

1. Pick any two baseball teams and compare them using a metric of your choice (average salary, home runs, number of wins, etc). Be creative! Write an SQL query to read in the table(s) you need, then use polars to manipulate the data. Finally, make a graph using Lets-Plot to visualize the comparison. What do you learn?

For this comparison, I chose two historic rivals, the New York Yankees and the Boston Red Sox, and looked at how many home runs each team hit per season since 2000. The `teams` table already includes total home runs (`HR`) by year, so I used that data and created a graph to compare the two teams over time.
One thing I noticed is that both teams had periods where their home run numbers increased and decreased, including the spike in home runs that occurred across the league in the late 2010s. The graph also makes it easy to see which team hit more home runs in a given season and how their offensive performance compared over the years.


```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
q = """
SELECT yearID, teamID, name, W, HR
FROM teams
WHERE teamID IN ('NYA', 'BOS') AND yearID >= 2000
ORDER BY yearID
"""
teams = pl.read_database(q, con)
df = teams.to_pandas()

(ggplot(df, aes(x='yearID', y='HR', color='name'))
 + geom_line(size=1)
 + geom_point(size=3)
 + labs(
     title='Home Runs per Season: Yankees vs. Red Sox (2000–present)',
     x='Year',
     y='Home Runs',
     color='Team')
 + theme_minimal())
```
